tagline.text: Volcanic islands off northern Luzon and Calayan's coastal scenery

location.label: Location
location.text: Northern Cagayan, Luzon Strait (main island Calayan, Poblacion)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱8,000–12,000 (basic 4-night, 5-day trip to Calayan, per person)

children.text: The Babuyan Islands are a cluster of volcanic and coral islands scattered across the Luzon Strait north of Luzon. Sibang Cove and Nagudungan Hill on Calayan are the most visited spots, and because boat trips depend on the weather, you need to plan with plenty of buffer time.

The Babuyan Islands are a group of about 24 volcanic and coral islands in the sea between the northern tip of Luzon and Batanes. The Babuyan Channel separates them from Luzon, and the Balintang Channel separates them from Batanes. The total area is given as about
590km²

, and the 2020 census counted roughly 19,000 residents. Administratively they belong to Cagayan province: Calayan, Camiguin, Dalupiri and Babuyan (Babuyan Claro) fall under the municipality of Calayan, while Fuga Island belongs to Aparri.
The five large islands are Calayan, Camiguin (Camiguin Norte), Dalupiri, Fuga and Babuyan Claro. Calayan is the largest (about
196km²

) and the most populated, so it is effectively the gateway and base for travel in the group. The eastern islands are part of the Luzon Volcanic Arc, and the Camiguin volcano, Babuyan Claro volcano and Smith volcano have all erupted in historical times. Mount Pangasun (1,108m) on Babuyan Claro is known as the highest peak in the group. In 1952 the Didicas volcano rose out of the sea and is now a permanent island.

The islands are also ecologically important. Calayan Island is home to the Calayan rail, a flightless bird recognized as a separate species in 2004 and found nowhere else. Dalupiri is home to the Ross' wolf snake, and both species are classified as critically endangered (CR). The waters are also a wintering ground for humpback whales, and conservation groups have pushed for national park and World Heritage status.

For travelers, the Babuyans are attractive precisely because they are hard to reach. There is no regular passenger ferry, and small outrigger boats (lampitaw) sail only when the weather and the Coast Guard allow. Your phone will lose signal and there are no ATMs. In return, you get Sibang Cove's wave-washed cream-colored sand, Nagudungan Hill where cows and goats graze, a cross-topped viewpoint on a hill, and waterfalls and sea caves that remain largely untouched on sparsely populated islands. In June 2026 a large expedition cruise ship (M/S Heritage Adventurer) again called at Calayan, and tourism is opening up little by little. This guide focuses on Calayan, the island most travelers actually visit.

This is Calayan's signature beach, known for cream-colored sand and strong waves. Rip currents form here and there are no lifeguards, so it is safest to swim only in shallow water. The nearby limestone formations and views over the Babuyan Channel also make it a popular photo spot.

A windswept grassy hill right next to Sibang Cove. Cows and goats graze here, a disused lighthouse remains, and the open views make sunset especially beautiful. There are no guardrails at the cliff edge and the wind is strong, so keep well back from the edge.
A hilltop with a cross, with an entrance fee of
that includes an escort guide. You can look down on Calayan Airport and the town. Both sunrise and sunset views are good.
These are waterfalls in the island's interior, and you must hire a local guide to reach them. Bataraw is reached by boat followed by a walk of about
10 minutes
, while Caanawan requires a long trek through dense forest on a rather muddy trail. The flow is usually fullest just after the rainy season.

Lusok Cave is a sea cave reachable only by boat and cannot be entered when the swell is high. Kannaway Cave is an inland cave with an underground pool inside. Both require a headlamp and non-slip shoes.
Where rocky cliffs meet the sea, popular with people who enjoy cliff jumping. You must go with a local guide, and water depth and waves vary day to day. Jump only from spots your guide approves.

You can see the island's birds around Magsidel and other areas. The flightless Calayan rail lives only on this island in the whole world, so it is not easy to see. Birding has the best chance of success early in the morning with a guide.

A boat tour around Smith Volcano, Babuyan Claro and Chinteb a Wasay. You charter a whole boat for a one-day trip, and it sails only when the waves and Coast Guard clearance allow. It is the best way to feel the volcanic landscape of the archipelago.

Pay the environmental and tourism fee at the municipal tourism office, drop your bags at your lodging, then head to Nagudungan Hill and Sibang Cove for sunset.
Rent a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) for the day and visit Bangaan Viewpoint, Tapwakan Cliff and Kannaway Cave. A guide is required for waterfalls and caves.
Tour Bataraw Falls and Lusok Cave by boat, or trek to Caanawan Falls. If the weather is bad, this day becomes your buffer day.
Take an early boat back to Claveria and board a bus to Manila. If sailing clearance is not given, it can take one more day, so leave slack in your return flight and work schedule.
It is safest to plan at least
2 days
on the island and to include one buffer day. A minimum itinerary is 4 days and 3 nights, but with no buffer day the schedule is easily thrown off.

children.text: Right after arriving on Calayan, discuss boat hire with the tourism office or your lodging. Whether the boat can sail depends on wave height and Coast Guard clearance.
Board the boat at Calayan port and head toward Babuyan Island and Smith Volcano. Boat hire costs about
, and splitting it among several people lowers the cost.
Land on the coast of Babuyan Claro, take in the scenery and have lunch, then pass Chinteb a Wasay on the way back.
Return to Calayan port before sunset. If your schedule has room, use your buffer day for this tour.

Calayan Airport opened in March 2019, and there are reports that Sky Pasada flies to Calayan from Laoag and Tuguegarao mainly on Tuesdays and Fridays. Baggage allowance is about
depending on the aircraft, and flights change often, so confirm directly with the airline.

items.title: Boat from Claveria or Aparri to Calayan

children.text: From Taggat Port in Claveria, M/B Macarra (0927 3277 889) and M/V Eagle Ferry (0947 773 3904) run to Calayan. The crossing takes about
4–6 hours
and the one-way fare is about
From Aparri Port, boats such as M/B Romina (0919 663 4954) run, taking about
6–7 hours
There is no fixed timetable, and boats usually depart between
and
. You must sign the Coast Guard passenger manifest, and your lodging can sometimes secure a seat for you.
During the northeast monsoon, the crossing can take as long as
7–9 hours
. Fares rise and fall with fuel prices, so check with the contact numbers before you leave.

items.title: Getting around the island and to other islands

children.text: There is no public transport on Calayan, so you rent a motorcycle, sidecar or tricycle for the day. A full-day habal-habal charter costs about
Other islands such as Babuyan Claro and Camiguin Norte have no regular service, so you must hire a boat from Calayan.
Fuga Island is reached by a separate route from Aparri, and because it is privately owned you need to check in advance.
The best time to visit the Babuyans is the dry season,
March–May
. The sea is calm and many crossings finish within
4–6 hours
, and there are reports of humpback whales passing in April and early May. Whale sightings are never guaranteed, however.
June–August

is the southwest monsoon and typhoon season. Sailings are often canceled, so allow plenty of buffer days. One traveler in late May to early June 2026 was stranded for two days by a typhoon passing nearby. From September to February the northeast monsoon brings high waves, and November and December are very wet, so most guides advise avoiding this period.

Homestays cluster in Calayan Poblacion. TPS Homestay (JP Rizal Street), Pagdagusan Homestay, Villa Inocencia Inn and San Jose Inn mostly charge around
per person per night, and Apollo Beach Resort in Dadao is listed at about
. Contact them ahead for the April–May peak season. Air-conditioned rooms can be used only when the power is stable and run around

Meals revolve around small eateries (carinderia) and homestay cooking. There are modest places such as Olen's Miki House (miki noodles) and Cafe Flora. Fresh-caught seafood and kinilaw are famous, so tell your host a day ahead and they will find fresh fish for you. Shops are few, so it is wise to buy snacks, bottled water and any medicine you need in Manila or Claveria.

CAGELCO II runs a solar hybrid system aimed at 24-hour power, but outages happen. Some past visitors reported power cuts from midnight until noon, so bring a power bank. Outlets are 220V, and types A, B and C are in use.
Bring plenty of cash. There are no ATMs or card terminals, and GCash works only when a Smart signal is available. Setting aside an extra
as an emergency reserve gives peace of mind.
Globe has virtually no signal, and Smart is weak and found only in the Poblacion. There is no signal at Sibang Cove, Nagudungan Hill or the waterfall trails, so download offline maps.
Build in buffer days and leave slack in your work and flight schedules. If the Coast Guard blocks sailing, you can be stranded for several days.
The boat is an open outrigger and you will get splashed. Pack your bag in a dry bag and bring a raincoat and seasickness pills. Some guides say the Coast Guard stops sailings when waves exceed about

On arrival, register first at the municipal tourism office (tourism officer Eric, 0947 893 9619) and pay the fee. Registration sometimes asks for your lodging and a local contact, so book a homestay in advance.

The Calayan LGU is reported to ban single-use plastics (bottles, cutlery, styrofoam) at beaches and trails under Executive Order No. 17 of 2025 (single source, confirm locally). Bring a reusable tumbler.
Do not go into the interior without a guide to the waterfalls and caves. A guide costs
per day and is cheaper when a small group splits it.
Boat fares have no standard rate and are tied to the livelihood of local fishers, so avoid bargaining too hard.
Sailing depends on the weather and Coast Guard clearance, and once blocked you can be stuck on the island for days. Check the latest weather bulletins and no-sail notices before crossing.
Sibang Cove has rip currents and no lifeguards. On days with strong waves, do not go into deep water.
Nagudungan Hill and the cliff viewpoints have no guardrails and strong winds. Keep away from the edge.
Emergency medical care is very limited. The Calayan Coast Guard station (0999-924-3554) is listed as the emergency contact. Bring your own first-aid supplies.
These are volcanic islands, so check eruption information and follow local guidance for places such as Babuyan Claro and Smith Volcano.
Fuga Island is privately owned and has a military detachment, so it is hard to enter freely. Confirm permission before you visit.
Fare and schedule information differs between older and newer reports (for example, one guide says boat fares rose from about ₱500 to ₱650–800). Check the latest information before you leave.
An island off the northeast coast of mainland Cagayan with beaches and a lighthouse. It combines well with a trip before or after the Babuyans.
A signature cave near Tuguegarao, and a good stop on the way back from the Babuyans.
Cagayan's central city and the airport hub. It serves as the transfer point to Claveria and Aparri.
A northern island province across the Balintang Channel, and a remote destination in the same northern seas as the Babuyans.
